claims.text: A combined first-principles transport workflow can calculate lattice and electronic thermal-transport channels separately.
Ab initio lattice dynamics can provide phonon dispersions and lifetimes for HfNbTaTiZr for use in a phonon Boltzmann calculation.
Electron relaxation times for HfNbTaTiZr can be determined through DFT/KRR-CPA approaches.
The proposed model will predict HfNbTaTiZr thermal transport to within 5–10% error.
Earlier Debye-type estimates had errors of approximately 50%.
Spark-plasma sintering of gas-atomized powder is a promising powder-metallurgy route for producing bulk, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr.
This processing route yields near-defect-free HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 0.1 wt.% oxygen.
Controlled HfNbTaTiZr variants containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen can be produced for comparison.
The model is applicable over 50–1200 K.
Oxygen impurities alter local vibrational modes and act as phonon-scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurity scattering modifies electronic states in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr will be nearly equal below 200 K.
Total thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K·m) between 300 and 1200 K.
Increasing oxygen content to approximately 1 wt.% will notably suppress the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution.
The electronic thermal-conductivity contribution will remain relatively unaffected by oxygen doping.
Previous analytical approaches conflated lattice and electronic transport through Debye approximations and defect-free simulations.
Substantial porosity or unintended grain-boundary changes would reduce the model's predictive applicability.
Determination of electron relaxation times is an important source of uncertainty in Boltzmann-transport calculations.
Uncertainty also arises from representing oxygen-induced defect configurations in HfNbTaTiZr.
Seebeck-coefficient analysis can independently provide the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution needed for the proposed falsification test.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises a reduction from approximately 50% error to 5–10% error, whereas the predicted outcome calls this only a 5–10% improvement. Those are materially different improvement magnitudes.

The structural mediator says oxygen modifies electronic states, while the predicted outcome assumes that the electronic contribution remains relatively unaffected; no distinction between state changes and negligible transport effects is supplied.
